questions.hint: Read the transition domain and acceptance condition carefully. Track which inputs are consumed and evaluate the whole word under the stated model.

answer.explanation: For a deterministic finite automaton, finite control receives the current state and input symbol and chooses the next state. Thus δ:Q×Σ→Q. A general NFA instead has a set of possible next states, so the stem tacitly uses the deterministic convention.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Outputs an input symbol, not a state.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The second input must be a symbol, not another state.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Omits the current state and uses two input symbols.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Correct deterministic domain and codomain.

evidence.quote: A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) is M=(Q,Σ,δ,q₀,F), with finite nonempty Q, start q₀∈Q, accepting set F⊆Q and total δ:Q×Σ→Q. Exactly one next state is specified per state/symbol pair; this does not mean the whole machine has one transition. F may be empty, recognizing ∅.

Start at q₀ and consume the entire input. Accept iff the ending state is in F; visiting an accepting state earlier is insufficient. ε is accepted exactly when q₀∈F. A nonaccepting sink loops on every symbol and cannot reach acceptance; it still finishes after finite input. Finite automata have finite memory encoded by states, not no state or no ability to remember any history.

answer.text: When the languages represented by both grammars are the same
answer.explanation: A grammar specifies its generated sentences. Equality of the generated sets, not equality of alphabets or overlap, is the criterion for semantic equivalence. For example {a} and {a,aa} have the same alphabet and a common string but different languages.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: One-way inclusion allows extra strings in the other language.

choices.label: B

evidence.quote: Write G=(V,Σ,P,S): finite variables V, terminals Σ disjoint from V, productions P and start variable S∈V. A production replaces its left side by its right side. The language is L(G)={w∈Σ*:S⇒*w}. A recognizer processes a word and accepts exactly the language members. Grammars generate languages; automata recognize languages, not grammars.
Two grammars are equivalent when their generated languages are equal, regardless of rule counts or variable names. One common word, equal alphabets or one-way inclusion is insufficient.

questions.hint: Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass.
sources: Computer Science model exam · Question 60
University of Gondar model exam · Question 60

answer.explanation: Ambiguity is witnessed by one terminal string having two distinct parse trees. It does not require every string to be ambiguous, and a string with no parse tree is simply not generated.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A unique tree is consistent with unambiguity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: No tree means failure to derive the string, not competing derivations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A partial tree is unfinished and does not witness two full derivations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Two or more full trees for the same string meet the definition.

evidence.quote: A CFG is ambiguous when some word has two distinct parse trees, equivalently two different leftmost derivations. Different expansion orders that give the same tree do not prove ambiguity.

Separate precedence levels: E→E+T|T, T→T*F|F, F→id|(E). Multiplication binds inside T before addition at E, and left recursion encodes left association. Uniqueness follows by the top-level last operator split and induction. S→SS|ε is already ambiguous for ε. S→A|B is ambiguous if A→ab and B→abB|ε both produce ab. Ambiguous grammar and inherently ambiguous language differ: another grammar may remove ambiguity.

questions.hint: Compare production restrictions, memory access and language-family containments. Distinguish an exact characterization from an included subclass.
sources: Computer Science model exam · Question 62

answer.explanation: A PDA augments finite control with a stack. Push and pop operations supply its unbounded LIFO memory.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A linked list is an implementation possibility, not the abstract PDA storage discipline.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A PDA uses stack memory.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hash lookup is not the PDA memory mechanism.

choices.label: D

evidence.quote: A nondeterministic pushdown automaton (PDA) adds a stack to finite control: (Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q₀,Z₀,F). Its transition relation maps (state,input symbol or ε,stack top) to possible (new state,replacement stack string) pairs.

A stack is last-in, first-out: push adds an item at the top and pop removes the top item, so the most recently pushed item is removed first. A PDA accesses this top rather than an arbitrary interior position.

A queue is first-in, first-out: insertion at the rear and removal at the front returns the oldest waiting item. A linked list can implement a storage discipline, but the implementation container is different from the abstract push/pop or enqueue/dequeue access rule.

answer.explanation: P is defined by deterministic polynomial-time decidability. NP, PSPACE and EXPTIME all contain P, so broad containment would not distinguish the choices. evidence.quote: Complexity classes here contain decision languages. evidence.quote: Complexity classes here contain decision languages. evidence.quote: A nondeterministic pushdown automaton (PDA) adds a stack to finite control: (Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q₀,Z₀,F). Its transition relation maps (state,input symbol or ε,stack top) to possible (new state,replacement stack string) pairs.

A stack is last-in, first-out: push adds an item at the top and pop removes the top item, so the most recently pushed item is removed first. A PDA accesses this top rather than an arbitrary interior position.

A queue is first-in, first-out: insertion at the rear and removal at the front returns the oldest waiting item. A linked list can implement a storage discipline, but the implementation container is different from the abstract push/pop or enqueue/dequeue access rule.

Hence every NP decision problem has a polynomial-time reduction to SAT. This starts the chain of later hardness reductions. A satisfying assignment can be checked in polynomial time. answer.explanation: An LBA checks block order then repeatedly marks one a, one b and one c, rejecting unmatched symbols. The language is not context-free, ruling out a PDA and therefore finite automata too.

evidence.quote: A context-sensitive rule αAβ→αγβ replaces A in context, with γ nonempty. Equivalently, noncontracting grammar presentations preserve/increase total length, with the isolated ε exception. The condition is on the complete sides, not an unrelated comparison |β|≥|α|.

A linear bounded automaton (LBA) is a TM with O(n) tape cells on length-n input; the standard CSL characterization uses nondeterministic LBAs. For aⁿbⁿcⁿ first verify a*b*c* order, repeatedly mark one unmarked a, b and c, and reject missing/excess symbols.

The two pieces v and y are pumped together; either may be empty, not both.
A non-CFL proof must defeat every allowed decomposition.
For s=aᵖbᵖcᵖ, the window vxy cannot contain both an a and a c. Pumping affects at most two blocks and at least one count.
Use i=0 or 2: the unaffected third block retains p while another count changes, or symbol order breaks.
Hence aⁿbⁿcⁿ is not CFL.
The copy language ww is also non-CFL over two symbols, whereas wwᴿ has the explicit grammar S→aSa|bSb|ε.
An expression that writes ww and calls it a palindrome is contradictory.

notes.title: Context-sensitive rules and linear bounded automata

blocks.text: A context-sensitive rule αAβ→αγβ replaces A in context, with γ nonempty.
Equivalently, noncontracting grammar presentations preserve/increase total length, with the isolated ε exception.
The condition is on the complete sides, not an unrelated comparison |β|≥|α|.
A linear bounded automaton (LBA) is a TM with O(n) tape cells on length-n input; the standard CSL characterization uses nondeterministic LBAs.
For aⁿbⁿcⁿ first verify a*b*c* order, repeatedly mark one unmarked a, b and c, and reject missing/excess symbols.
All marks stay within the input region.
A fixed input has finitely many configurations, at most |Q|m|Γ|ᵐ for m cells.
Reachability search in that finite graph decides acceptance, even if some machine branches loop.
Thus every CSL is decidable.

a*b* and {aⁿb:n≥0} are regular. aⁿbⁿ is CFL but not regular.
Over a two-symbol alphabet, wwᴿ is CFL, ww is not CFL; both are decidable. aⁿbⁿcⁿ is CSL but not CFL, and therefore decidable.
Every finite language is regular.
A stronger grammar or TM can still recognize any of these lower-family languages.

Every unary CFL is regular, so this language is not CFL either.
It is nevertheless context-sensitive: count the input in bounded workspace and test divisors.

δ(q,a)=(p,b,L) means read a in q, write b, move one cell left and enter p. Accept/reject halting states have no further moves under this convention.

notes.title: TM design, variants and computation limits

blocks.text: To decide aⁿbⁿcⁿ, repeatedly mark matching triples, resetting the head between scans, then verify no unmatched symbol remains.
Each round marks additional input cells, so finitely many rounds suffice.
To decide ww, reject odd length, locate the midpoint using marks/counters, and compare corresponding symbols of the two halves; writable tape permits access a single stack lacks.
State both the acceptance test and why every input halts.
An off-line TM has a read-only input tape and separate read/write work tape.
Multitape, multihead, two-way-infinite-tape and nondeterministic TMs have the same language-recognition power as standard TMs, though simulation costs differ.
Two unbounded stacks can simulate a tape.
Turing completeness means ability to simulate general TM computation, not polynomial speed or literally using infinitely many cells in a finite run.
The Church–Turing thesis connects effective procedures to this formal model; it is not a proved runtime theorem.

A decider halts on every input and accepts exactly its language; these languages are recursive/decidable.
A recognizer must halt and accept every member, but on a nonmember may halt-reject or loop.
Its languages are recursively enumerable (RE), Turing-recognizable or semidecidable.
Looping is nonacceptance, not a rejecting halt.
An undecidable language may still have a recognizer.
Every decidable language is RE, and the containment is strict.
If L and its complement are both RE, simulate their recognizers in dovetailed steps until one accepts, obtaining a decider.
Conversely complementing a decider works because it always halts.
Flipping final states in an arbitrary recognizer fails to handle nonmembers that loop.
Recursive function theory's total computable functions are not merely programs written with recursive self-calls; partial computable functions may be undefined where computation does not halt.

HALT={⟨M,w⟩:M halts on w} is recognizable: simulate and accept upon any halt.
Suppose a decider H determines halting.
Construct D(x) that loops if H(x,x) says halt, otherwise halts.
Running D on its own description contradicts H in both cases.
Thus HALT is undecidable and witnesses RE beyond DECIDABLE.
Its complement is not RE, or both recognizers would yield a decider.

blocks.text: Time counts computation steps; space counts cells/memory used, specifying whether read-only input is excluded.
For a deterministic decider use the maximum over all length-n inputs; for a time-bounded nondeterministic decider every branch meets the bound.
Big-O is an asymptotic upper bound, not inherently a worst-case label: it can describe a worst-, average- or best-case function. Θ adds a matching lower bound.

Encoding matters: the number N in binary has Θ(log N) bits, so O(N) work is not polynomial in its binary input length.

A verifier must accept some certificate exactly for yes-inputs; no certificate may falsely establish a no-instance.

notes.title: NP-hard versus NP-complete; decision versus optimization

blocks.text: X is NP-hard if every A∈NP satisfies A≤pX.
It need not belong to NP and can even be undecidable.
X is NP-complete if X∈NP and X is NP-hard.
NP-complete languages lie inside NP and can be decided by finite exhaustive certificate search in exponential time.
They are not known to require exponential time.
SAT asks whether a Boolean formula has a satisfying assignment; Cook–Levin establishes SAT NP-complete.
CNF-SAT and 3-SAT are NP-complete versions.
TSP decision asks whether a tour of cost at most B exists; it is NP-complete for standard finite encoded inputs.
Finding the shortest tour is optimization and NP-hard; call it NP-complete only after specifying a decision formulation.
Fixed 2-colorability is in P, while fixed k-colorability for k≥3 is NP-complete.

For a 3-CNF formula with m clauses, make one vertex for each literal occurrence.
Connect two vertices iff they come from different clauses and are not complementary literals.
Ask whether the graph has a clique of size m. Construction takes polynomial time and space.
A satisfying assignment supplies one true literal per clause; they are mutually consistent and form a clique.
Conversely an m-clique selects one occurrence per clause, with no variable chosen both positively and negatively, so assign those literals true and extend remaining variables arbitrarily.
Both implications prove equivalence.

NP⊆PSPACE because candidate polynomial witnesses can be enumerated and checked one at a time, reusing memory; exponentially many candidates do not require retaining them all.

notes.title: The stack discipline and its queue contrast

blocks.text: A stack is last-in, first-out: push adds an item at the top and pop removes the top item, so the most recently pushed item is removed first. A PDA accesses this top rather than an arbitrary interior position.

A queue is first-in, first-out: insertion at the rear and removal at the front returns the oldest waiting item. A linked list can implement a storage discipline, but the implementation container is different from the abstract push/pop or enqueue/dequeue access rule.

notes.title: Why satisfiability was the first NP-complete problem

blocks.text: Boolean satisfiability was the first problem proved NP-complete, through the Cook–Levin theorem. Its hardness proof starts directly from an arbitrary nondeterministic polynomial-time computation and constructs a Boolean formula that is satisfiable exactly when an accepting computation exists.

This starting point matters: once one NP-complete problem is available, later hardness proofs can reduce that known problem to a new target. Membership in NP remains a separate obligation. Checking a satisfying assignment is efficient; whether finding one is always polynomial-time remains unresolved.

notes.title: Finite procedures are different from undecidable tasks

blocks.text: Sorting a finite numeric list is a terminating computation. Quicksort, for example, chooses a pivot, partitions the other entries and recursively sorts the smaller sublists. Each recursive subproblem has fewer entries. A large running time does not make the task undecidable.

A finite linear system with exactly represented rational coefficients can be processed by Gaussian elimination and back substitution. Row exchanges handle unsuitable pivots; row reduction detects inconsistency or leaves free variables describing multiple solutions. These finite algebraic procedures differ from a general halting decider, which does not exist.
